questions.question_text: What is the Cartesian equation of the curve defined by $x = 3t + 1$ and $y = 6t - 5$?

options.why: Forgot to distribute the gradient multiplication into the constant term of $t=(x-1)/3$.
Subtracted $2$ from $-5$ instead of evaluating $2(-1)-5=-7$.
Used $6/2=3$ as the gradient instead of dividing $6$ by $3$ to get $2$.

questions.question_text: Convert the parametric equations $x = 2t - 4$ and $y = 5t + 1$ to general form $Ax + By + C = 0$.

options.why: Rearranged $x = 2t - 4$ as $t = \dfrac{x - 4}{2}$, subtracting the $4$ instead of adding it, giving $2y = 5x - 20 + 2$.
Inverted the gradient to $\dfrac{2}{5}$ instead of $\dfrac{5}{2}$, then used the point $(-4, 1)$ from $t = 0$.
Inverted the gradient to $\dfrac{2}{5}$ and also took the $t = 0$ point as $(4, 1)$ by misreading $x = 2t - 4$.

questions.question_text: What is the Cartesian equation of the curve $x = 4p,\; y = p^2 + 2$ with $y$ as the subject?

options.why: Did not square the denominator $4$ when substituting $p=x/4$.
Multiplied by $16$ instead of dividing by $16$.
Changed the sign of the constant $+2$ to $-2$.

questions.question_text: Convert the parametric equations $x = t + 2$ and $y = 3t^2 - 4t + 1$ to Cartesian form.

options.why: Subtracted $8$ instead of adding $+8$ from the expansion of $-4(x-2)$.
Replaced $t$ directly with $x$ without applying the shift $t=x-2$.
Omitted the linear term expansion from $-4(t)$.

questions.question_text: What is the Cartesian equation of the curve $x = 3 + 6\cos\theta$ and $y = -2 + 6\sin\theta$?

options.why: Copied the centre signs straight from the parametric equations instead of reversing them inside each bracket.
Wrote the radius $6$ on the right-hand side instead of squaring it to get $r^2 = 36$.
Copied the centre signs unchanged into the brackets and also left the radius unsquared as $6$.

questions.question_text: Convert the parametric equations $x = -4 + 5\cos\theta$ and $y = 1 + 5\sin\theta$ to Cartesian form.

options.why: Read the centre as $(-1, 4)$ by taking the constant from the wrong equation for each coordinate.
Placed the radius $5$ on the right-hand side instead of $r^2 = 25$.
Took the constants from the wrong equation for each coordinate and also left the radius unsquared as $5$.

questions.question_text: Which Cartesian equation corresponds to the parametric equations $x = 4t$ and $y = \dfrac{8}{t}$ for $t \ne 0$?

options.why: Divided $8$ by $4$ instead of multiplying the parametric equations together.
Substituted $t=x/4$ incorrectly as $y=8/(4/x)=2x$.
Mistook the reciprocal product form for a circle equation.

questions.question_text: Convert the parametric equations $x = 2 + t^2$ and $y = 3 - t$ for $t \ge 0$ to Cartesian form with its correct restrictions.

options.why: Omitted the required domain and range restrictions generated by $t \ge 0$.
Incorrectly concluded $y \ge 3$ instead of $y = 3 - t \le 3$ for $t \ge 0$.
Used an invalid domain inequality $x \le 2$ where the radicand would be negative.

questions.solution_text:
$t = 3 - y$
$x = 2 + (3 - y)^2$
Since $t \ge 0$, $3 - y \ge 0 \implies y \le 3$.
Since $t^2 \ge 0$, $x = 2 + t^2 \ge 2$.
$x = 2 + (3 - y)^2$ with $y \le 3$ and $x \ge 2$
